## {{< iconify clarity group-solid >}} What is a Population?

A *population* is a collection of individuals or observations we are
interested in. This is also commonly denoted as a study population in science research, or a *target audience* in design. We
mathematically denote the population's size using upper-case `N`.

A *population parameter* is some numerical summary about the population
that is unknown but you wish you knew. For example, when this quantity
is a mean like *the mean height of all Bangaloreans*, the population
parameter of interest is the *population mean* $\mu_{pop}$.

A *census* is an exhaustive enumeration or counting of all N individuals
in the population. We do this in order to compute the population
parameter's value exactly. Of note is that as the number N of
individuals in our population increases, conducting a census gets more
expensive (in terms of time, energy, and money).

::: callout-important
## {{< iconify carbon parameter >}} Parameters

Populations *P*arameters are usually indicated by Greek Letters.
:::

## {{< iconify game-icons card-pickup >}} What is a Sample?

Sampling is the act of collecting a small subset from the population,
which we generally do when we can't perform a **census**. We
mathematically denote the sample size using lower case `n`, as opposed
to upper case `N` which denotes the population's size. Typically the
sample size `n` is much smaller than the population size `N`. Thus
sampling is a much cheaper alternative than performing a census.

A **sample statistic**, also known as a *point estimate*, is a summary
statistic like a `mean` or `standard deviation` that is computed from a
sample.

::: callout-note
## Why do we sample?

Because we cannot conduct a census ( not always ) --- and **sometimes we
won't even know how big the population is** --- we take samples. And we
*still* want to do useful work for/with the population, after estimating
its parameters, *an act of generalizing* from sample to population. So
the question is, **can we estimate useful parameters of the population,
using just samples? Can point estimates serve as useful guides to
population parameters?**

[This act of generalizing from sample to population is at the heart of
**statistical inference**.]{style="background-color: yellow;"}
:::

::: callout-important
## An Alliterative Mnemonic

NOTE: there is an
[*alliterative*](https://www.grammarly.com/blog/alliteration/)
[*mnemonic*](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/mnemonic) here:
**S**amples have **S**tatistics; **P**opulations have **P**arameters.
:::

## {{< iconify fluent-mdl2 test-parameter >}} Population Parameters and Sample Statistics

|                    | Population Parameter | Sample Statistic |
|--------------------|----------------------|------------------|
| Mean               | $\mu$                | $\bar{x}$        |
| Standard Deviation | $\sigma$             | s                |
| Proportion         | p                    | $\hat{p}$        |
| Correlation        | $\rho$               | r                |
| Slope (Regression) | $\beta_1$            | $b_1$            |

: Parameters and Statistics

Some examples:

::: callout-note
## Question

Q.1. What is the mean commute time for workers in a particular city?

A.1. The *parameter* is the mean commute time $\mu$ for a *population*
containing all workers who work in the city. We *estimate* it using
$\bar{x}$, the mean of the random sample of people who work in the city.
:::

::: callout-note
## Question

Q.2. What is the correlation between the size of dinner bills and the
size of tips at a restaurant?

A.2. The *parameter is* $\rho$ , the correlation between bill amount and
tip size for a *population* of all dinner bills at that restaurant. We
estimate it using r, the correlation from a random sample of dinner
bills.
:::

::: callout-note
## Question

Q.3. How much difference is there in the proportion of 30 to 39-year-old
residents who have only a cell phone (no land line phone) compared to 50
to 59-year-olds in the country?

A.3. The *population* is all citizens of the country, and the parameter
is $p_1 - p_2$, the difference in proportion of 30 to 39-year-old
residents who have only a cell phone ($p_1$) and the proportion with the
same property among all 50 to 59-year olds ($p_2$). We estimate it using
($\hat{p_1} - \hat{p_2}$), the difference in sample proportions computed
from random samples taken from each group.
:::

Sample statistics vary and in the following we will estimate this
uncertainty and decide how reliable they might be as estimates of
population parameters.

## {{< iconify mdi head-thinking-outline >}} {{< iconify clarity group-solid >}} So What do We Want?

Let us define the purpose we have in mind:

- We want to estimate the population parameters, such as the population mean $\mu$ and the population standard deviation $\sigma$.
- We want to take ***just one sample*** from the population, and compute the sample statistics such as the sample mean $\bar{x}$ and the sample standard deviation $s$.
- (Because that is all we can afford, let us say). 
- We want to be sure that estimates from the sample are not very much off from the population parameters.
- And we want to know how to quantify that uncertainty. 


To achieve this purpose, we need a certain amount of theoretical justification. Let us now dig into those systematically. 

## {{< iconify mdi head-thinking-outline >}} {{< iconify clarity group-solid >}} An "Assumed" Population

First something counter-intuitive: we need to *define a population* for the sake of reference. We will use the `NHANES` dataset, and pick one variable out it it, `Height`, and treat it as our population.

```{r}
#| label: read_data
#| code-fold: true
#| 
data("NHANES")
NHANES %>% glimpse()
```


Let us create a NHANES (sub)-dataset without duplicated IDs and only
adults and select the `Height` variable:

```{r}
#| label: data_select
#| code-fold: true
#| 
NHANES_adult<-  
  NHANES %>%
  distinct(ID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>% 
  filter(Age >= 18) %>% 
  select(Height) %>% drop_na(Height)
NHANES_adult

```

::: callout-important
## An "Assumed" Population

We will now onwards **treat** this single-variable dataset as our **Population**. So this is our *population*, with appropriate *population parameters* such as `pop_mean` = $\mu$, and `pop_sd` = $\sigma$.
:::

Let us calculate the **population parameters** for the `Height` data
from our "assumed" population:

```{r}
#| label: pop-params
# NHANES_adult is assumed population
pop_mean <- mosaic::mean(~ Height, data = NHANES_adult)
pop_sd <- mosaic::sd(~ Height, data = NHANES_adult)
pop_mean
pop_sd

```
Let us now start our sampling game!


### {{< iconify game-icons card-pickup >}} Sampling

Now, we will sample **ONCE** from the `Height` variable. Let us
take a sample of `sample size` n = 50. We will compare **sample statistics**
with **population parameters** on the basis of this ONE sample of n = 50:

:::: {layout="[ 40, 60 ]"}

::: {#first-column}
```{r}
#| label: single-sample-50-data
#| warning: false
#| code-fold: true
#| 

set.seed(12345) # for reproducibility
sample_50 <- mosaic::sample(NHANES_adult, size = 50) %>% 
  select(Height)
sample_50

sample_mean_50 <- mean(~ Height, data = sample_50)
sample_mean_50

```

A Single Sample of size 50.
:::

::: {#second-column}
```{r}
#| label: fig-single-sample
#| fig-cap: Distribution and Mean of a Single Sample
#| code-fold: true
#| 
# Plotting the histogram of this sample
ggplot2::theme_set(new = theme_custom())
sample_50 %>% 
  gf_histogram(~ Height, bins = 10) %>% 
  
  gf_vline(xintercept = ~ sample_mean_50, 
           color = "purple") %>% 
  
  gf_vline(xintercept = ~ pop_mean, 
           colour = "black") %>% 
  
  gf_annotate("label", y = 7, x = pop_mean - 8, 
          label = "Population Mean", 
          color = "black") %>% 
  
  gf_annotate("label", y = 7, x = sample_mean_50 + 8, 
          label = "Sample Mean", color = "purple") %>% 
  
  gf_annotate("curve", 
          x = sample_mean_50 + 8, y = 6.5, 
          xend = sample_mean_50 + 1, yend = 2,
          curvature = -0.2, color = "purple", 
          arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.5,"cm"))) %>% 
  
  gf_annotate("curve", 
          x = pop_mean - 8, y = 6.5, 
          xend = pop_mean - 1, yend = 2,
          curvature = 0.2, color = "black", arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.5,"cm"))) %>% 
  
  gf_labs(y = "Frequency",
          title = "Distribution and Mean of a Single Sample",
          subtitle = "Sample Size = 50")


```
:::

::::


### {{< iconify ic baseline-loop >}} {{< iconify game-icons card-pickup >}} {{< iconify icon-park-outline average >}} Repeated Samples and Sample Means

OK, so the `sample_mean_50`($\bar{x}$) is not too far from the
`pop_mean` ($\mu$). Is this ***always*** true, i.e. for ***any sample***? 

Let us check: we will create 500 repeated samples, each of size 50. And calculate their mean as the *sample statistic*, giving us a data frame containing 500 `sample means` ($\bar{x}$-s). We will then see if ***all these 500 means*** lie close to the `pop_mean`($\mu$):

```{r}
#| label: 500-samples-of-50-each
#| layout: [[75], [25]]
#| warning: false
#| code-fold: true

sample_50_500 <- do(500) * {
  sample(NHANES_adult, size = 50) %>%
    select(Height) %>% # drop sampling related column "orig.id"
    summarise(
      sample_mean = mean(Height),
      sample_sd = sd(Height),
      sample_min = min(Height),
      sample_max = max(Height))
}
sample_50_500 <- 
  sample_50_500 %>% 
  select(index = .index, sample_min, sample_max, sample_mean, sample_sd)
sample_50_500
dim(sample_50_500)

```


```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| label: fig-sample-means-sds
#| fig-cap: Sample Means and SDs
#| fig-subcap: 
#|  - Sample Means 
#|  - Sample SDs
#| code-fold: true
ggplot2::theme_set(new = theme_custom())

sample_50_500 %>%
  gf_point(index ~ sample_mean, color = "purple",
           title = "Sample Means are close to the Population Mean",
           subtitle = "Sample Means are Random!",
           caption = "Grey lines represent our 500 samples") %>%
  
  gf_segment(
    index + index ~ sample_min + sample_max,
    color = "grey",
    linewidth = 0.3,
    alpha = 0.3,
    ylab = "Sample Index (1-500)",
    xlab = "Sample Means"
  ) %>%
  
  gf_vline(xintercept = ~ pop_mean, 
           color = "black") %>%
  
  gf_annotate("label", y = -25, x = pop_mean, 
              label = "Population Mean", 
              color = "black") 

##

sample_50_500 %>%
  gf_point(index ~ sample_sd, color = "purple",
           title = "Sample SDs are close to the Population SD",
           subtitle = "Sample SDs are Random!",) %>%
  
  gf_vline(xintercept = ~ pop_sd, 
           color = "black") %>%
  
  gf_annotate("label", y = -25, x = pop_sd, 
              label = "Population SD", 
              color = "black") %>% 
  gf_refine(lims(x = c(4,16))) %>% 
  gf_labs(x = "Sample SDs", y = "Sample Index (1-500)")

```

::: callout-note
### Sample Means and Sample SDs are a Random Variables!![^8]

The `sample_mean`s (the $\bar{x}$-s, purple dots @fig-sample-means-sds-1) are all generally in the vicinity of the `pop_mean` ($\mu$, vertical black line). And since they are themselves random [because the samples are random]{.black .bg-yellow}, they will have [their own distribution]{.bg-yellow .black}, with a `mean` and `sd` too, over all the 500 sample-means. 

And the `sample_sd`(the $s$-s) are also random (see @fig-sample-means-sds-2) and [have their own distribution](https://www.researchgate.net/post/Standard_Deviation_Distribution/59032925ed99e1ba910f11ff/citation/download), around the `pop_sd` ($\sigma$).[^5]. This distribution of the sample-sds will also have its own `mean` and `sd` too !!

Are you confused yet? Hold tight! `r emoji::emoji("scream")` `r emoji::emoji("scream")` `r emoji::emoji("scream")` `r emoji::emoji("scream")`
:::

[^8]: <https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Introductory_Statistics/Introductory_Statistics_(Shafer_and_Zhang)/06%3A_Sampling_Distributions/6.01%3A_The_Mean_and_Standard_Deviation_of_the_Sample_Mean>

[^5]: <https://mathworld.wolfram.com/StandardDeviationDistribution.html>

### {{< iconify game-icons card-pickup >}} {{< iconify tabler chart-histogram >}} Distribution of Sample-Means

So now let's plot the **distribution** of these 500 sample-means themselves, called [**a distribution of sample-means**]{.bg-yellow .black}. We will also plot the position of the population mean `pop_mean` parameter $\mu$, the mean of the `Height` variable.

::: callout-note
WHY? Because we want to see how the sample-means are distributed around the population mean, and how they compare with the population distribution itself.
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-Sampling-Mean-Distribution
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| code-fold: true
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: Sample Mean Distribution
#| fig-subcap: 
#|  - Sample Means Distribution
#|  - Sample Means Distribution overlaid with Population Distribution
ggplot2::theme_set(new = theme_custom())

sample_50_500 %>% 
  gf_dhistogram(~ sample_mean, bins = 30, xlab = "Sample Means only") %>% 
  
  gf_vline(xintercept = pop_mean, 
           color = "blue") %>% 
  
  gf_label(0.01 ~ pop_mean, 
            label = "Population Mean", 
            color = "blue") %>% 
gf_labs(title = "Sample Means are Distributed around Pop. Mean!",
        subtitle = "500 means")


# How does this **distribution of sample-means** compare with the
# overall distribution of the population?
# 
sample_50_500 %>% 
  gf_dhistogram(~ sample_mean, bins = 30, xlab = "Sample Means, and the Height variable") %>% 
  
  gf_vline(xintercept = pop_mean, 
           color = "blue") %>% 
  
   gf_label(0.01 ~ pop_mean, 
            label = "Population Mean", 
            color = "blue") %>% 

  ## Add the population histogram
  gf_histogram(~ Height, data = NHANES_adult, 
               alpha = 0.2, fill = "blue", 
               bins = 30) %>% 
  
  gf_label(0.045 ~ (pop_mean + 20), 
           label = "Population Distribution\n of Height", 
           color = "blue") %>% 
gf_labs(title = "Sample Means are Close Together!", 
        subtitle = "Compare Original Population overlay!")


```


### {{< iconify carbon concept >}} Deriving the Central Limit Theorem (CLT)


-   We see in the @fig-Sampling-Mean-Distribution-1 above that the *distribution of sample-means* is centered around the
    `pop_mean` $\mu$. ( *Mean of the sample means* = `pop_mean` $\mu$!! `r emoji::emoji("scream")`)
-   And from @fig-Sampling-Mean-Distribution-2 that the "spread" aka `sd` of the *distribution of sample means* is within than population itself. [Well within](https://www.alice-in-wonderland.net/resources/chapters-script/alices-adventures-in-wonderland/chapter-7/) ! Curiouser and curiouser! 
-   But exactly how much is it? And what is the kind of distribution?
-   Why are we interested? *Any single sample* needs to give us an estimate for `pop_mean` $\mu$. And it had better be good, with small standard deviation. 
- And does the sample ***size*** matter? Does the sample mean distribution change if we take a larger sample?

One more experiment. 

Now let's repeatedly sample `Height` and compute the sample-means ( $\bar{x}$-s), and
look at the resulting histograms. (We will deal with sample-standard-deviations shortly.) We will also use sample sizes $n$ = `c(8, 16, 32, 64)` and generate 1000 samples each time, take the means and plot these 4 * 1000 means:

:::: {layout="[25,25, 25, 25]"}

::: {#first-column}
```{r}
#| code-fold: true
set.seed(12345)
samples_08_1000 <- do(1000) * resample(NHANES_adult$Height, 
                                       size = 08) %>% 
                   mean() 
samples_08_1000 <- samples_08_1000 %>% 
                   dplyr::rename("mean" = result) # rename the column
samples_08_1000

```
Means of 1000 samples of size 8
:::

::: {#second-column}
```{r}
#| code-fold: true
set.seed(12345)
samples_16_1000 <- do(1000) * resample(NHANES_adult$Height, 
                                       size = 16) %>% mean()
samples_16_1000 <- samples_16_1000 %>% 
                   dplyr::rename("mean" = result) # rename the column
samples_16_1000

```
Means of 1000 samples of size 16
:::

::: {#third-column}
```{r}
#| code-fold: true
set.seed(12345)
samples_32_1000 <- do(1000) * resample(NHANES_adult$Height, 
                                       size = 32) %>% mean()
samples_32_1000 <- samples_32_1000 %>% 
                   dplyr::rename("mean" = result) # rename the column
samples_32_1000
```
Means of 1000 samples of size 32
:::

::: {#fourth-column}
```{r}
#| code-fold: true
set.seed(12345)
samples_64_1000 <- do(1000) * resample(NHANES_adult$Height, 
                                       size = 64) %>% mean()
samples_64_1000 <- samples_64_1000 %>% 
                   dplyr::rename("mean" = result) # rename the column
samples_64_1000
```
Means of 1000 samples of size 64
:::

::::


```{r}
#| warning: false
#| eval: false
#| echo: false

ggplot2::theme_set(new = theme_custom())

# Now let's create separate Q-Q plots for the different sample sizes.
p1 <- gf_qq( ~ mean, data = samples_08_1000,
             title = "N = 8", 
             color = "dodgerblue") %>%
  gf_qqline()

p2 <- gf_qq( ~ mean, data = samples_16_1000,
            title = "N = 16", 
            color = "sienna") %>%
  gf_qqline()

p3 <- gf_qq( ~ mean, data = samples_32_1000,
            title = "N = 32", 
            color = "palegreen") %>%
  gf_qqline()

p4 <- gf_qq( ~ mean, data = samples_64_1000,
            title = "N = 64", 
            color = "violetred") %>%
  gf_qqline()

cowplot::plot_grid(p1, p2, p3, p4)

# The QQ plots show that the results become more normally distributed
# (i.e. following the straight line) as the samples get larger. 
```

Let us plot their individual histograms to compare them:

```{r}
#| label: fig-sampling-distributions
#| fig-cap: Sampling Distributions
#| fig-subcap: 
#|   - Sample Size = 8
#|   - Sample Size = 16
#|   - Sample Size = 32
#|   - Sample Size = 64
#| fig-asp: 0.618
#| warning: false
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| layout-nrow: 2
#| code-fold: true
ggplot2::theme_set(new = theme_custom())

# Let us overlay their individual histograms to compare them:
p5 <- gf_dhistogram(~ mean,
              data = samples_08_1000,
              color = "grey",
              fill = "dodgerblue",title = "N = 8", xlab = "Sample Means") %>%
  gf_fitdistr(linewidth = 1) %>%
  gf_vline(xintercept = pop_mean, inherit = FALSE,
           color = "blue") %>%
  gf_label(-0.025 ~ pop_mean, 
           label = "Population Mean", 
           color = "blue") %>% 
  gf_theme(scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.08,0.02))))
##
p6 <- gf_dhistogram(~ mean,
              data = samples_16_1000,
              color = "grey",
              fill = "sienna",title = "N = 16", xlab = "Sample Means") %>%
  gf_fitdistr(linewidth = 1) %>%
  gf_vline(xintercept = pop_mean,
           color = "blue") %>%
  gf_label(-.025 ~ pop_mean, 
           label = "Population Mean", 
           color = "blue") %>% 
  gf_theme(scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.08,0.02))))
##
p7 <- gf_dhistogram(~ mean,
                    data = samples_32_1000 ,
                    na.rm = TRUE,
                    color = "grey",
                    fill = "palegreen",title = "N = 32", xlab = "Sample Means") %>%
  gf_fitdistr(linewidth = 1) %>%
  gf_vline(xintercept = pop_mean,
           color = "blue") %>%
  gf_label(-.025 ~ pop_mean, 
           label = "Population Mean", color = "blue") %>%
```

From the histograms we learn that the sample-means are **normally distributed** around the *population mean*. [This feels intuitively right
because when we sample from the population, many values will be close to
the *population mean*, and values far away from the mean will be
increasingly scarce.]{style="background-color: yellow;"}

Let us calculate the means of the 4 **sample-mean-distributions**:

::::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
#| label: sample-means
#| eval: false

mean(~ mean, data  = samples_08_1000) # Mean of means!!!;-0
mean(~ mean, data  = samples_16_1000)
mean(~ mean, data  = samples_32_1000)
mean(~ mean, data  = samples_64_1000)
pop_mean

```
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
```{r}
#| ref.label: sample-means
#| echo: false
```
:::
:::::

All are nearly identical, and also pretty close to the population mean !!! So regardless of sample size, we get an estimate of the `pop_mean` from the mean of a sample! Whoo-Hoo!!! But how good can the estimate be? How much uncertainty is there in this estimate?

For that, we need to look at the *standard deviations* of the 4 sampling-mean distributions:

$$
\Large{sd_i = \sqrt{\frac{\Sigma^{1000}_{k} {[{mean_k} - \overline{mean_k}}]^2}{n_i}}}~, i = 1...4
$$

::::: columns
::: column
We take the sum of all *squared [differences]{.bg-washed-red .black}* from the mean in a sample. If we divide this sum-of-squared-differences by the sample length $n$, we get a sort of *average squared difference*, or *per-capita* squared error from the mean, which is called the **variance**.

Taking the square root gives us an average error, which we would call, of course, the *standard deviation*.
:::

::: column
```{r}
#| label: showing-variance-calculation
#| echo: false
ggplot2::theme_set(new = theme_custom())

sample_50 %>% 
  rowid_to_column() %>% 
  gf_hline(yintercept = mean(~sample_50$Height)) %>% 
  gf_segment(mean(Height) + Height ~ rowid + rowid, colour = "red") %>% 
  gf_point(Height ~ rowid) %>% 
  gf_labs(x = "Observation Index", y = "Sampled Height",
  title = "Sum of Squares of Red lines/n = Variance",
subtitle = "Black Line = Mean")

```
:::
:::::


::::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
#| label: sample-distribution-sds
#| eval: false

pop_sd
sd(~ mean, data  = samples_08_1000)
sd(~ mean, data  = samples_16_1000)
sd(~ mean, data  = samples_32_1000)
sd(~ mean, data  = samples_64_1000)

```
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
```{r}
#| ref.label: sample-distribution-sds
#| echo: false
```
:::
:::::

These are also decreasing steadily with sample size. How are they related to the `pop_sd`?

::::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
#| label: sample-dist-sds-popsd
#| eval: false

pop_sd
pop_sd /sqrt(8)
pop_sd / sqrt(16)
pop_sd / sqrt(32)
pop_sd / sqrt(64)

```
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
```{r}
#| ref.label: sample-dist-sds-popsd
#| echo: false
```
:::
:::::

::: callout-important
### SD of Sample-mean-distribution reduces with $1/sqrt(n)$
As we can see, the *standard deviations* of the **sampling-mean-distributions** is inversely proportional to the square root of lengths of the sample. Which means that as we increase the sample size of our planned single sample, the *standard deviation* of the sample-mean-distribution decreases, and so does the uncertainty in our estimate of the `pop_mean`!
:::

::: callout-note
## Central Limit Theorem

Now we have enough to state the **Central Limit Theorem (CLT)**

-   the [sample-means are normally distributed around the *population
    mean*]{style="background-color: yellow;"}. So any mean of a **single sample** is a good, **unbiased estimate** for the `pop_mean`.
    
    $$
    \Large{\bar{x} \sim pop.mean }
    $${#eq-clt-mean}

-   the **sample-mean distributions** are centered around the `pop_mean` and have a *standard deviation* that is [inversely proportional to the square root of the sample size.]{style="background-color: yellow;"}. 

    $$
    \Large{s \sim \frac{pop.sd}{sqrt(n)} }
    $${#eq-clt-sd}

-   This is [regardless of the distribution of the *population*]{style="background-color: yellow;"} itself.[^1]
:::

[^1]: The `Height` variable seems to be normally distributed at
    population level. We will try other non-normal population variables
    as an exercise in the tutorials.

This theorem underlies all our procedures and techniques for statistical inference, as we shall see.

:::{}
<center>
{{< video https://youtu.be/_YOr_yYPytM width=560 height=360 >}}
</center>
Understanding the Central Limit Theorem
:::


## {{< iconify dashicons code-standards >}} The Standard Error

Consider once again the *standard deviations* in each of the **sample-mean-distributions** that we have generated. As we saw, these are smaller than the `pop_sd` $\sigma$, and decrease with sample size:

`sd = pop_sd/sqrt(sample_size)` where sample-size[^4] here is
one of `c(8, 16, 32, 64)`.

[^4]: Once `sample size = population`, we have complete access to the
    population! So ALL SAMPLES ARE IDENTICAL to the POPULATION, and so `sample_sd = 0`; there is no question of estimation error!

::: callout-important
We reserve the term *Standard Deviation* for the population sd, $\sigma$, and name
this computed standard deviation of the sample-mean-distributions as the
**Standard Error**. This statistic derived from the sample-mean-distribution will help us infer our population parameters with a precise estimate of the *uncertainty* involved.
:::


$$
\Large{Standard\ Error\ \pmb {se} =  \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt[]{n}}}\\
$${#eq-standard-error}

[However, we don't normally know the `pop_sd`!! So now what?? So is this chicken and egg??]{style="background-color: yellow;"}

## {{< iconify game-icons card-pickup >}} Back to One Sample!!

Remember, we are poor, and lazy. Let us take **SINGLE SAMPLES** of each size, as we normally would:

::::: columns
::: {.column width="85%"}
```{r}
#| label: single-samples
#| eval: false
#| 
set.seed(1963)
sample_08 <- mosaic::sample(NHANES_adult, size = 8)
sample_16 <- mosaic::sample(NHANES_adult, size = 16)
sample_32 <- mosaic::sample(NHANES_adult, size = 32)
sample_64 <- mosaic::sample(NHANES_adult, size = 64)
##
pop_sd
sd(~ Height, data = sample_08)
sd(~ Height, data = sample_16)
sd(~ Height, data = sample_32)
sd(~ Height, data = sample_64)
  
```

:::

::: {.column width="15%"}


```{r}
#| ref.label: single-samples
#| echo: false
```
:::
:::::


::: callout-warning
### Distribution of Sample SDs
As we saw at the start of this module, the sample-means are distributed around the `pop_mean`, AND it appears that the sample-sds are also distributed around the `pop_sd`! 

However, the sample-sd distribution is **not Gaussian** (because an sd can never be negative), and the sample_sd is also **not an unbiased estimate** for the `pop_sd`. However, when the sample size $n$ is large ($n >= 30$), the sample-sd distribution approximates the Gaussian, and the bias is small. 
:::

And so, in the same way, [we approximate the `pop_sd` with the sd of a **single sample** of the same length]{style="background-color: yellow;"}. Hence the *Standard Error* can be computed from **a single sample** as:

$$
\boxed{\Large{Standard\ Error\ \pmb {se} \sim \frac{sample.sd}{\sqrt[]{n}}}}
$${#eq-standard-error}

With these, the Standard Errors(SE) evaluate to:

::::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}

```{r}
#| label: standard-error-computation
#| eval: false

pop_sd
sd(~ Height, data = sample_08) /sqrt(8)
sd(~ Height, data = sample_16) /sqrt(16)
sd(~ Height, data = sample_32) /sqrt(32)
sd(~ Height, data = sample_64) /sqrt(64)

```
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
```{r}
#| ref.label: standard-error-computation
#| echo: false
```
:::
:::::

Why are we concerned with Standard Errors(SE)? Because they are the **uncertainty** in our sample-mean estimates of the population mean. And when we want to be **more certain**, we need to reduce the SE and therefore...make our sample larger. Design hack!

## {{< iconify fluent auto-fit-width-24-filled >}} Confidence intervals

When we work with samples, we want to be able to speak with a certain
degree of confidence about the **population mean**, based on the
evaluation of **one** sample mean, not a large number of them. Given
that sample-means are *normally distributed* around the `pop_mean` $\mu$, we can say that:

- $68\%$ of *all possible sample-mean-s* lie within
$\pm 1* SE$ of the *population mean*; 
- $95 \%$ of *all possible sample-mean-s* lie within $\pm 2 * SE$ of the *population mean*. 
- These two multiplier-constants $\pm 1$ and $\pm 2$ are the `z-scores` from the *z-distribution* we saw earlier[^9].

[^9]: We know $\Large{z_{score} = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu}{SE}}$, 
and so $\bar{x} = \mu + z_{score} * SE$, which tells us ***how far*** our sample mean is from $\mu$.


```{r}
#| label: fig-confidence-intervals-examples
#| layout-ncol: 3
#| fig-cap: Confidence Intervals Examples
#| fig-subcap: 
#|   - 68% Confidence Intervals
#|   - 95% Confidence Intervals
#|   - 95% CIs from Multiple Samples
#| code-fold: true
#| 
set.seed(42) # Not a good idea always!
###
mosaic::xqnorm(p = c((1-0.68)/2, 1 - (1-0.68)/2), 
               return = c("plot"), verbose = F,
               system = "gg", pattern = "rings",
               alpha = 0.5, colour = "black",) %>% 
  gf_labs(x = "Z-score (Increments of SE)", title = "68% Confidence Intervals") %>% gf_refine(scale_x_continuous(breaks = -4:4))
###
mosaic::xqnorm(p = c((1-0.95)/2, 1 - (1-0.95)/2), 
               return = c("plot"), verbose = F, 
               system = "gg", pattern = "rings",
               alpha = 0.5, colour = "black") %>% gf_labs(x = "Z-score (Increments of SE)", title = "95% Confidence Intervals") %>% gf_refine(scale_x_continuous(breaks = -4:4))
###
TeachingDemos::ci.examp(mean.sim = 100, sd = 2,n = 50, reps = 50, method = "z")

```

In @fig-confidence-intervals-examples-3, we see that $95\%$ confidence intervals straddle the population mean shown in black, almost always. For a particular sample with $\bar{x} === 100$, the vertical red lines show the confidence interval derived from *that* sample.  One sample in 50 has missed it and is shown in [pink]{.black .bg-pink}.


## CI and Sample Size

How do these vary with sample size $n$?

```{r}
tbl_1 <- get_ci(samples_08_1000, level = 0.95)
tbl_2 <- get_ci(samples_16_1000, level = 0.95)

  rownames_to_column("index") %>% 
cbind("sample_size" = c(8,16,32,64)) %>% 
gf_segment(index + index ~ lower_ci + upper_ci, linewidth = 1) %>% 
gf_vline(xintercept = pop_mean, colour = "blue", linewidth = 2) %>%

        subtitle = "Varying samples sizes 8-16-32-64",
        y = "Sample Size", x = "Mean") %>%
```

Yes, with sample size! Why is that a good thing?

So:

- Every sample we could take sets up a Gaussian distribution for the estimate of the `pop_mean` $\mu$. (Which is `sample_mean` $\bar{x}$ in this case.)
- Each sample will have a different `sample_mean` $\bar{x}$, and therefore the distribution curves, being centred on `sample_mean` would move to the right or to the left. 
- Each such sample distribution sets up a Confidence Interval. 
- [We expect that 95% out of all the samples will setup a Confidence Interval that contains the `pop_mean` $\mu$]{style="background-color:yellow;"}.
- THEREFORE, any one of all those samples is good enough and all that we need!!!

## {{< iconify flat-color-icons workflow >}} CLT Workflow

Thus if we want to estimate a *population mean*:

-   we take one **random** sample from the population of length $n$
-   we calculate the mean from the `sample_mean` $\bar{x}$
-   we calculate the `sample_sd` $s$
-   we calculate the *Standard Error* as $\frac{s}{\sqrt[]{n}}$
-   we calculate 95% confidence intervals for the *population parameter* based on the formula
    $CI_{95\%}= \bar{} \pm 2*SE$.
- So finally, 
$$ 
\boxed{\Large{\mu \sim \bar{x} \pm 2.0 * \frac{s}{\sqrt[]{n}}}} $${#eq-pop-mean-estimate}
    
## {{< iconify flat-color-icons workflow >}} CLT Assumptions

- Population Standard Deviation $\sigma$ is known;
- Sample is of "decent length" $n >= 30$;
- Therefore sample histogram is Gaussian.

When these are violated, as with small sample sizes, or with unknown population sds, we need to use the *t-distribution* instead of the *z-distribution* to calculate confidence intervals. The *t-distribution* is a family of distributions that are similar to the Gaussian, but have heavier tails. This leads to slightly wider Confidence Intervals being computed.

## {{< iconify mingcute thought-line >}} Wait, But Why?

- We want to take **one sample** from a population and use it to make inferences about population `parameters`
- We compute a `statistic` from the sample, i.e. a `mean`
- We want to be able to say how accurate it is, i.e. state its `mean` and `standard deviation`, and the `relative probability` of how probable the `statistic` could be
- Relative probabilities, means, and standard deviations are only possible to calculate if we have ***many*** means, and therefore, ***many*** samples!!
- So we, as [frequentist]{style="background-color:yellow;"} people, ***pretend*** we can take many samples and calculate the `mean of the means` and the `standard deviation of the means` (Now called `standard error`), and the `relative probability` of a the calculated `statistic`
- These tell us how the `mean`s are distributed and how accurate the `mean-mean` can be
- Since `standard error` uses the (unknown and unknowable) `population sd`, we approximate that by `sample sd`
-   Since Standard Error decreases with sample size, we need to make our sample of adequate size.( $n=30$ seems appropriate in most cases. Why?)
-   And we do not have to worry about the distribution of the
    population. It need not be normal/Gaussian/Bell-shaped !!

    Biology".
    <https://www.middleprofessor.com/files/applied-biostatistics_bookdown/_book/>
1.  Adam Loy, Lendie Follett & Heike Hofmann (2016) Variations of
    *Q*--*Q* Plots: The Power of Our Eyes!, The American Statistician,
    70:2, 202-214, DOI:
    [10.1080/00031305.2015.1077728](https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.2015.1077728)
